newsitem.title: ICELAND: Scientists hope for new picture of Iceland volcano.
newsitem.headline: Scientists hope for new picture of Iceland volcano.

text.p: Icelandic scientists were hoping on Wednesday for their first glimpse in four days of an erupting volcano that has melted parts of a glacier, threatening to flood a vast, uninhabitated plain.

After a long-awaited break in atrocious weather conditions that grounded monitoring crews, scientists were preparing to fly over the huge, isolated Vatnajokul glacier, Europe's largest glacier, on the island's southeast coast.
"From seismic measurements of earth tremors of the eruption site we know the eruption is still going on," Pall Imsland, a geologist with Iceland University, told Reuters.
"But it is difficult to interpret the seismic data, or at least correlate it with the actual eruption, because we have not been able to see what's going on up there.
"Today we hope to make a flight and reevaluate the prospects of the flood."

Iceland has been bracing for massive flooding since the sub-glacial volcano erupted 10 days ago, bursting through the desolate glacier last Wednesday and firing out a six km (20,000 feet) high tower of smoke and gas.

Scientist have been using aerial measurements to assess the volume of ice melted by the eruption which is located some 250 kms (150 miles) east of the capital of Reykjavik and about the same distance south of the Arctic Circle.

Weekend assessments indicated that about two trillion litres (400 billion gallons) of water had collected in the Grimvotn subglacial lake -- enough to cover a square mile of surface to a depth of half a mile.
The water level is rising by 10 metres (33 feet) each day, putting increasing pressure on the glacier's ice cap which is crackingly ominously and is expected to burst under the strain.

Scientists said the size of the earth tremors due to the movement of liquid rock, or magma, have declined over the past few days which could mean the eruption was less vigorous or that the flowing magma was meeting less resistance.
But whether the eruption has slowed or not, large scale flooding, not seen since a similar eruption at the same spot in 1938, was inevitable, scientists said.
"There's no doubt the lake will flood but the timing of the onset is the uncertainty," said Magnus Tumi Gudmundsson, head or aerial monitoring and geophysicist at Iceland University.
"This (uncertainty) has grown the longer we have been unable to visually assess the eruption site."
It is estimated the water from the brimming lake will surge out in torrents of up to 25 metres per second, flooding the surrounding black sand plain, uninhabitated but for sheep.

The volcano's eruption has caused an eight km (fibe mile) long fissure running north to northeast along the glacier and a depression of up to two kms (a mile) in the ice that lies in the shadow of Mount Eystrafjall.
Most of the ash spewed out by the volcano has collected under the ice cap, forming a mountain about 200 metres (650 feet) tall.

The area, declared an emergency zone, remains deserted except for the occasional group of journalists and government workers trying to prepare the ground to protect the country's one coastal ring road, which passes through this small settlement southwest of the glacier, from the flood.
Iceland was site of one of the greatest lava flows in a single eruption in the history of the world in 1783, when the volcano Lakagigar erupted. The damage led to huge famine.
